items.title: Marks 8–11: Self-Mark, Common Mark, and the Coarse-and-Calm Pair

items.zh: 云何自相相？謂自類自相，或各別自相。此所思惟，名自相相。云何共相相？謂諸行共相，或有漏共相，或一切法共相。此所思惟，名共相相。
items.en: What is the self-mark? The self-mark of a class, or the individual self-mark. This reflection is the self-mark. What is the common mark? The common mark of formations [impermanence], or the common mark of the contaminated [suffering], or the common mark of all dharmas [emptiness and non-self]. This reflection is the common mark.

items.zh: 云何麁相？謂所觀下地一切麁相。云何靜相？謂所行上地一切靜相。
items.en: What is the coarse mark? All the coarse marks of a lower ground, contemplated. What is the calm mark? All the calm marks of a higher ground, ranged over.

items.title: Marks 12–16: Past, Future, and Present, and the Defiled and Undefiled Mind

items.zh: 云何領納相？謂隨憶念過去曾經諸行之相。云何分別相？謂思未來諸行之相。云何俱行相？謂分別現在諸行之相。云何染污相？謂於有貪心思惟有貪心相，乃至於不善解脫心思惟不善解脫心相。云何不染污相？謂與此相違，當知即是不染污相。
items.en: What is the mark of receiving? Recollecting the marks of formations passed through in the past. What is the mark of discrimination? Thinking on the marks of future formations. What is the mark of accompaniment? Discriminating the marks of present formations. What is the defiled mark? Contemplating, in a craving mind, the mark of a craving mind — up to contemplating, in an ill-liberated mind, the mark of an ill-liberated mind. What is the undefiled mark? Know it to be the reverse of this.

items.zh: 此中已出離於斷不修方便者，觀有貪等；修方便者，觀略下等。有貪心者，謂貪相應心，或復隨逐彼品麁重。如是由纏及隨眠故，一切染污心如應當知以能對治纏及隨眠故，成不染污。
items.en: Herein, one who has [worldly] release but does not cultivate the means for severance observes [only] the craving mind and the rest; one who cultivates the means observes the contracted, the sunken, and so on. The craving mind is the mind associated with craving, or trailed by that category's coarse unfitness; thus, by manifestation and by latent tendency, every defiled mind is to be known accordingly. Because one can counter both manifestation and latent tendency, the mind becomes undefiled.

items.title: Marks 17–20: Right and Wrong Method, Luminosity, and Investigation

items.zh: 云何正方便相？謂所思惟白淨品因緣相相。云何邪方便相？謂所思惟染污品因緣相相。即是思惟如是如是不守根門住故，乃至不正知住故，如是如是心被染相。
items.en: What is the mark of right method? The contemplated mark of the causal mark of the bright-and-pure category. What is the mark of wrong method? The contemplated mark of the causal mark of the defiled category — that is, contemplating how, by not guarding the sense-doors, and so on up through not dwelling with clear comprehension, the mind comes in just such a way to be defiled.

items.zh: 云何光明相？謂如有一，於暗對治或法光明、慇懃懇到善取其相，極善思惟。如於下方，於上亦爾。如是一切治暗相故，建立此相。云何觀察相？謂有苾芻、慇懃懇到善取其相而觀察之。住觀於坐者，謂以現在能取觀未來所取法。坐觀於臥者，謂以現在能取觀過去所取。或法在後行觀察前行者，謂以後後能取觀前前能取法。
items.en: What is the mark of luminosity? As when someone, [seeking] the antidote to darkness or the light of the Dharma, earnestly and thoroughly takes up its mark and contemplates it well. As below, so above. Thus, because it is entirely the mark that treats darkness, this mark is established. What is the mark of investigation? A monk who earnestly and thoroughly takes up the mark and investigates it. "Standing observing sitting" is using the present grasping-mind to observe the future object-to-be-grasped. "Sitting observing lying" is using the present grasping-mind to observe the past object. "Or, in a later act observing an earlier act" is using each later grasping-mind to observe each earlier grasping-mind.

items.zh: 此則略顯二種所取、能取法觀。

items.title: Marks 21–25: Wholesome Concentration, and the Four Real-Time Adjustments

items.zh: 云何賢善定相？謂所思惟青瘀等相，為欲對治欲貪等故。何故此相說名賢善？諸煩惱中貪最為勝，於諸貪中欲貪為勝，生諸苦故。此相是彼對治所緣，故名賢善。
items.en: What is the mark of wholesome concentration? The contemplated marks of the bruised-blue corpse and the rest, in order to counter the craving of desire and the like. Why is this mark called "wholesome"? Among the afflictions craving is foremost, and among cravings the craving of sexual desire is foremost, for it produces all sufferings; this mark is the object that counters it, and so is called "wholesome."

items.zh: 云何止相？謂所思惟無分別影像之相。云何舉相？謂策心所取隨一淨妙或光明相相。云何觀相？謂聞思修慧所思惟諸法相。云何捨相？謂已得平等心，於諸善品增上捨相。
items.en: What is the calming mark? The contemplated mark of a non-discriminated image. What is the uplifting mark? Spurring the mind to take up some pure-sublime or luminous mark. What is the insight mark? The marks of phenomena contemplated by the wisdom of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. What is the equanimity mark? Having attained an even mind, the mark of a heightened equanimity towards the wholesome factors.

items.title: Marks 26–32: Entering, Abiding, Emerging, Increase, Decrease, Method, and Eliciting

items.zh: 云何入定相？謂由因緣、所緣、應修習相故入三摩地，或復已得而現在前。云何住定相？謂即於彼諸相善巧而取；由善取故，隨其所欲於定安住。又於此定得不退法。云何出定相？謂分別體所不攝不定地相。
items.en: What is the mark of entering concentration? Entering samādhi by means of the causal mark, the object-mark, and the mark-to-be-cultivated; or, having attained it, its coming to be present. What is the mark of abiding in concentration? Skilfully taking up those marks, and by that skilful taking-up, abiding in concentration at will; and attaining the non-retrogressing state in that concentration. What is the mark of emerging from concentration? The mark of the unconcentrated ground, not included [in concentration], as taken up by the discriminating substance, the mind itself.

items.zh: 云何增相？謂輕安定倍增廣大所思惟相。云何減相？謂輕安定退減陜小所思惟相。云何方便相？謂二道相。或趣倍增廣大，或趣退減陜小故。云何引發相？謂能引發略諸廣博文句義道，若無諍、無礙、妙願智等，若依三摩地諸餘力、無畏等最勝功德，及能通達甚深句義、微妙智慧，如是等相。
items.en: What is the mark of increase? The contemplated mark of pliancy and concentration doubling and expanding. What is the mark of decrease? The contemplated mark of pliancy and concentration receding and shrinking. What is the mark of method? The mark of the two paths, tending either towards doubling-and-expanding or towards receding-and-shrinking. What is the mark of eliciting? The mark that can elicit the way of compressing vast phrasing and meaning [and expanding it], as well as non-contention, unobstructedness, the wondrous knowledge-of-vows, and — based on concentration — the [ten] powers, fearlessnesses, and other supreme qualities, and the penetration of the profoundest phrasing-and-meaning and subtlest wisdom.

items.title: All Thirty-Two Marks Folded Back into the Four

items.zh: 復次，如是諸相即前根本四相所攝，謂所緣相、具攝一切。因緣相亦爾。前與後為因緣故，為令後後得明淨故。正方便相一切種別，皆因緣相。如正方便，邪方便亦爾。一是白品相，第二黑品相。諸染污相唯應遠離。所餘諸相唯應修習。於彼彼時應修習故。
items.en: Furthermore, all these marks are subsumed under the four root marks stated earlier. The object-mark subsumes them all. The causal mark likewise — since each earlier one serves as the cause of the later, making each successive mark clearer and purer. The mark of right method, in all its varieties, is entirely the causal mark; and as with right method, so with wrong method — the one a bright-category mark, the second a dark-category mark. The defiled marks are only to be avoided; the remaining marks are only to be cultivated, since at each occasion they are to be cultivated.

blocks.text: The last reading of fascicle 11 completes the thirty-two marks a meditator cultivates. The list covers the whole arc of a meditation session: what to contemplate, how to adjust, how to enter, stay, and emerge, and how to tell whether practice is growing or declining. It then folds all thirty-two back into the four marks of Day 84.

Marks eight to sixteen are themes of insight: the **self-mark** and **common mark** of things (Day 1's particular and shared marks); the **coarse and calm** marks, by which one compares a lower level with a higher (the basis of the seven root attentions); the marks of **past, future, and present**; and the **defiled and undefiled** mind.

Marks seventeen to twenty: **right and wrong method**; **luminosity**; and **investigation**. In investigation, the treatise says one observes "the present observing the future", explained with an obscure phrase (住觀於坐) that Venerable Miào Jìng reads concretely: 住 is the present posture, standing, and 坐 the posture to come, sitting. One observes the body and mind in the present while knowing the next moment is already arriving.

Mark twenty-one is **wholesome concentration**, exemplified by the bruised-corpse contemplation. Master Cháng Bǎi explains why this is called "wholesome": "Among cravings, sexual craving is strongest, producing every kind of suffering"; the impure mark counters it, as breath mindfulness counters discursive thought.

Marks twenty-two to twenty-five are four adjustments during a session: when the mind sinks, lift it; when it rises, calm it; when it is balanced, leave it alone in equanimity; when it is drawn by pleasure, see the fault. These are the "four real-time adjustments" every meditation teacher gives in some form.

Marks twenty-six to thirty-two: **entering**, **abiding**, and **emerging** from concentration; its **increase** and **decrease**; the **method**; and **eliciting** (引發), drawing out the qualities concentration makes possible, such as the supernormal powers and insight. A skilled meditator knows how to enter and leave deliberately, and can tell whether practice is improving or slipping.

The treatise closes by folding the thirty-two back into the four marks of the object: the object, its causes, what to avoid, and what to cultivate. The long list and the short list describe the same practice at different resolutions.

Fascicle 11 has given the framework of meditation: the four dhyānas and their factors; the five hindrances and what feeds and starves each; the release of feelings level by level; the four reliances; the seven root attentions and forty attentions; and the object with its thirty-two marks. Fascicles 12 and 13 complete the Stage of Meditative Absorption, with more detail on the concentrations and on how to practise them.

quiz.q: In the mark of investigation, 住觀於坐 is rendered "present observing the future-sitting." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain 住 and 坐?
options: 住 is the present posture (standing), soon to sit; 坐 is the future posture — not a seated mind
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "住 is the present posture; after standing a while one will sit — 坐 is the future posture." The text: this "is using the present grasping-mind to observe the future object-to-be-grasped." The note's "seated grasping-mind" and the translation lose the posture (logged).

quiz.q: Why is the bruised-corpse mark called "wholesome concentration," per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: sexual craving is the strongest and breeds all suffering; the impure mark counters it, hence "wholesome" — impurity and breath contemplation were the two gates of nectar
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Among cravings, sexual craving is strongest, producing every kind of suffering"; "the impure mark is the object that counters it, so it's called wholesome; in early Buddhism impurity and breath contemplation were the two gates of nectar." The text: craving is foremost among afflictions.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, which wisdoms go with attention on the letter and attention on the meaning?
options: attention on the letter goes with wisdom from hearing; on the meaning, with wisdom from reflection and cultivation
quiz.why: "Attention on the teaching-letter is the attention associated with the wisdom born of hearing. Attention on the meaning is the attention associated with the wisdom born of reflection and cultivation." Venerable Miào Jìng: one can't contemplate ultimate truth apart from the words.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, which abidings do the five and the six gateways belong to?
options: of the five: first four heavenly, fifth noble; of the six: first four Brahmā-abidings, fifth and sixth noble
quiz.why: "Of the former five gateways … the first four are subsumed under the heavenly abidings, and the fifth alone under the noble abidings. Of the present six … the first four under the Brahmā-abidings, and the fifth and sixth under the noble abidings." Venerable Miào Jìng: heavenly abidings are the dhyānas; the noble cut self-view.

quiz.q: "Equanimity counters craving and ill will, proceeding as 俱捨." The translation says letting go of both. How does Master Cháng Bǎi read it?
options: an even mind towards all beings, without favour or grudge, neither elated nor grieved — that is 俱捨
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "An even mind towards all beings, not closer to some or resentful of others — this counters craving and ill will. Neither elated nor grieved — that is 俱捨." He cites Tsongkhapa's verse on equanimity. The translation's "lets go of both" reads it differently (logged).
